To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

attractiveness bias can influence our perceptions of intelligence and academic performance, and that perceived conscientiousness is a more accurate predictor than intelligence and academic performance.

(1) perceived conscientiousness is a more accurate predictor for actual academic performance than perceived intellectual performance and perceived overall academic performance, and (2) the accuracy of perceived academic performance is improved when controlling for attractiveness bias.

attractiveness bias can lead to inaccurate judgments of academic performance, that perceived conscientiousness is a better predictor of academic performance compared to perceived intelligence, and that perceived conscientious is more accurate when controlling for attractiveness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the attractiveness bias on the accuracy of perceptions of academic performance and the role of conscientiousness in this process.
the impact of attractiveness bias on accuracy of first impressions and its impact on the accuracy of judgments of academic performance.
the accuracy of first-impressions based on facial stimuli and how attractiveness can influence the accuracy of these first-impressions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
attractiveness is an inaccurate cue for assessing academic performance and perceived conscientiousness is more accurate than perceived intelligence.
attractiveness is a poor predictor of actual intelligence, but a better predictor of perceived conscientiousness.
attractiveness does have a significant impact on the accuracy of perceptions of actual academic ability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

attractiveness does influence our judgments of academic performance, and the effect of attractiveness on judgments is stronger when the judgment is based on intelligence, rather than conscientiousness.
we have found that attractiveness does influence the accuracy of perceptions of academic performance.
we investigated the accuracy of first impression judgments based on facial cues and found that attractiveness bias is a limiting factor in accurately judging intelligence and conscientiousness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the attractiveness halo effect can have a detrimental influence on the accuracy of our judgments of competence.
the attractiveness halo is a powerful bias in the accuracy of first impression judgments.

attractiveness is a poor cue for assessing academic performance, and we should look beyond attractiveness to other facial cues to make accurate first impressions. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2020 APA, all rights reserved)
